title: Novena for Couples Longing for a Child
kicker: 9 days of hope in the waiting
card: For married couples who long for a child: 9 days of honest prayer, hope in the waiting, and a marriage held close to God.
ogDescription: 9 days of prayer for couples longing for a child, through Our Lady, St. Joachim, St. Anne and St. Zechariah.
description: A 9-day Catholic novena for married couples longing for a child, through Our Lady of Hope, St. Joachim, St. Anne and St. Zechariah.

epigraph.text: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us.

closingVerse.text: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

printClosing: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing,
so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

saints.name: St. Joachim
saints.bio: Father of the Virgin Mary. Scripture does not name him; an ancient tradition says that he and Anne long had no child, and that he went into the wilderness to fast and pray.
saints.alt: Fresco: St. Joachim, sorrowful, holding a lamb, by Giotto
saints.openingRole: who knew the sorrow of waiting

saints.name: St. Anne
saints.patron: Invoked by couples hoping for a child
saints.bio: Mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus. An ancient tradition tells of her years without a child, her tears and prayer, and Mary’s birth as God’s gift to her and Joachim.
saints.alt: Fresco: St. Anne kneeling in prayer, by Giotto

saints.name: St. Zechariah
saints.patron: Father of St. John the Baptist
saints.bio: A priest who, with his wife Elizabeth, lived blamelessly before God yet had no child into old age. When an angel said his prayer was heard, he doubted, and was silent until John was named.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Zechariah writing his son’s name, by a Dutch master after Rogier van der Weyden
saints.openingRole: who served You faithfully through long years

openingPrayer: Heavenly Father, Giver of every life, You know N. and the child they long for. You see the years of hoping, the prayers that seem unanswered, the tears they share and the tears they hide. We bring this longing to You with open hands. Grant them, if it is Your will, the gift of a child, and in every season keep their love for each other strong. Today we ask Our Lady of Hope; St. Joachim, who knew the sorrow of waiting; St. Anne, who prayed through her tears; and St. Zechariah, who served You faithfully through long years, to join their prayers with ours, through Christ our Lord.
closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, You welcomed the little children and wept with those who mourn. Hold N. close to Your heart. Make their marriage fruitful in love, give them peace while they wait, and let Your holy will be done.

tips.p: One person leads each part; all respond pray for us and Amen, and say the closing prayers together. The prayers say “we”; if you pray alone, say “I”.

If you can, go to Confession and attend Mass together during these 9 days, and ask a priest to bless your marriage. Look for doctors who seek and treat the causes of infertility (often called restorative reproductive medicine); a priest can help you think through hard medical choices (Day 6). A medal or relic is a sign of prayer, not a charm. At “N.”, say the couple’s names, or “us” if you pray for yourselves.

Years of waiting, or the loss of a pregnancy, can weigh on body, mind and marriage. It is never a sign that you prayed too little (Day 2). A counselor, a support group or your parish can help, and a priest can pray with you after a loss (Day 7); the Church has a blessing for parents after a miscarriage or stillbirth, and funeral rites for the baby. If sorrow ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out right away to someone you trust or a crisis helpline.

tips.h: Praying for a couple you love
tips.p: Pray quietly, and let them share only what they want to. Skip the questions about plans and the advice about what worked for someone else; “I’m praying for you” is often enough. Remember them on Mother’s Day, Father’s Day and at christenings, which can be hard days.

intentionPlaceholder: Write the couple’s names and the graces you ask for them.

days.title: Pouring Out Our Hearts
days.verse: She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD, and wept bitterly.
days.refl: Hannah longed for a child for years. At the shrine of Shiloh she did not hide her pain or tidy up her words; she wept and poured out her heart before the Lord. Many couples know that ache: the hope each month, the disappointment, the tests and treatments, the silence after another try. God does not ask us to pretend we are fine. He invites us to come to Him as Hannah did, honestly and with tears. So we begin these nine days by laying our whole longing before Him.
days.more: Hannah’s story opens the First Book of Samuel. Her husband loved her, yet her husband’s other wife provoked her year after year, and when she prayed in silence, the priest Eli took her for a drunken woman (1 Samuel 1:6–13). She kept praying anyway. Mary’s mother bears the same name, for Anne comes from the Hebrew name Hannah. Both women bring us the same lesson: no prayer is too raw for God.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, You heard Hannah when she wept before You at Shiloh, and You hear N. today. We bring You their longing for a child, their hope and their weariness, and every prayer they no longer know how to say. Through the prayers of Our Lady of Hope and St. Anne, give them courage to pour out their hearts to You, and the peace of knowing that no tear of theirs is hidden from You.
days.step: Tell God plainly, in your own words, what you long for and how tired you are. Then pray one Hail Mary together.

days.title: Not a Punishment
days.verse: And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
days.refl: Luke tells us two things about Zechariah and Elizabeth side by side: they were righteous before God, and they had no child. In their day many took childlessness as a sign of God’s displeasure, and Elizabeth spoke of the reproach she had carried (Luke 1:25). Luke’s Gospel sets that idea aside. Not being able to conceive is not a punishment, and it does not measure our faith or our worth. Today we let go of any guilt we carry, and receive again God’s love for us.
days.more: Some couples quietly blame themselves: for waiting too long, for a past sin, for their own bodies. If an old sin weighs on you, bring it to Confession and leave it there; God’s mercy is complete. Infertility is a medical condition, not a verdict on anyone’s soul. The Catechism says simply that couples who discover they are sterile “suffer greatly” (CCC 2374). The Church does not ask them to hide that suffering.
days.prayer: Lord God, Zechariah and Elizabeth walked faithfully before You through long years without a child. Free N. from every false guilt and every whisper of shame. Where they need Your mercy, let them receive it gladly; where they blame themselves for what is not their fault, let them hear Your voice of love. Through the prayers of St. Zechariah and St. Anne, help them believe that they are Your beloved children, now and always.
days.step: Name one thing you blame yourself for, and hand it over to God. If it is a sin, plan to bring it to Confession.

days.title: Holding Each Other
days.verse: And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?”
days.refl: Elkanah loved Hannah, and he could not fix her sorrow. His words were tender and a little clumsy, as words often are when two people hurt in different ways. Waiting for a child can strain even a strong marriage. One spouse wants to talk and the other goes quiet; one is ready for the next step, the other needs to rest; tests and calendars crowd out tenderness. Today we pray that this waiting will draw husband and wife closer, not push them apart.
days.more: An ancient tradition tells that while Joachim fasted in the wilderness, Anne grieved alone at home, and that each was comforted before they met again at the city gate, the scene Giotto painted as a tender embrace. Their story reminds us that a couple’s love is itself a gift. The Church teaches that a marriage without children can still radiate a fruitfulness of charity, hospitality and sacrifice (CCC 1654).
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You blessed the wedding at Cana; bless the marriage of N. When they grieve in different ways, give them patience with each other. When the waiting wears them down, renew their tenderness and their friendship. Through the prayers of St. Joachim and St. Anne, let their love grow deeper in this trial, and let each of them find in the other a place of rest, never one more burden.
days.step: Spend fifteen minutes together today without talking about having a baby. Ask each other, “How are you really doing?”, and listen.

days.title: When Others Don’t Understand
days.verse: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.
days.refl: Few things sting like a careless question: “So when are you having kids?” Baby announcements, christenings and family gatherings can bring real joy for others and fresh pain for us in the same moment. St. Paul asks us to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, and that is hard when we are the ones weeping. Today we ask for the grace to be gentle with others and with ourselves, and for friends who will weep with us.
days.more: An ancient tradition tells that Joachim brought his offering to the Temple and was turned away because he had no child. Ashamed, he did not go home but went into the wilderness to fast and pray for forty days. Many couples know that feeling of standing outside while others celebrate. It is all right to skip a gathering you cannot bear today, and to tell people kindly that you would rather not discuss it.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, You know the questions that sting and the celebrations that are hard to bear. Guard N. from bitterness, and give them grace to rejoice with others when they can and to rest when they cannot. Through the prayers of St. Joachim, who knew shame and found You in the wilderness, send them friends who listen without judging, and teach all of us to speak with kindness and to listen with love.
days.step: Prepare one short, kind answer to the question that hurts most. Then pray today for another couple who is also waiting.

days.title: The Long Wait
days.verse: I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, / and in his word I hope; / my soul waits for the LORD / more than watchmen for the morning, / more than watchmen for the morning.
days.refl: Watchmen on a city wall cannot make the sun rise. They keep watch through the dark, trusting that morning will come. Waiting for a child can feel like a long night counted in months and years. The psalmist does not tell us the night is short. He tells us where to put our hope: in the Lord and in His word. Today we ask for strength to keep watch with Him, one day and one month at a time.
days.more: Zechariah served as a priest year after year, offering prayer for his people while his own prayer for a child seemed to go unanswered. When the angel finally came, he found it hard to believe, and he was left unable to speak until John was named (Luke 1:18–20, 59–64). Yet God did not take back His gift because of his doubt. He is patient with ours, too, when the waiting makes hope hard.
days.prayer: Lord God, You are faithful through every night. Strengthen N. in this long waiting. When their hope runs thin, hold it for them; when they are too tired to pray, receive even their silence as a prayer. Through the prayers of Our Lady of Hope and St. Zechariah, who served You faithfully through many years, keep their hearts watching for You like watchmen for the morning, and give them peace for today.
days.step: Before you sleep tonight, pray today’s verse slowly, and offer God all the months you have already waited.

days.title: Wisdom for Hard Choices
days.verse: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all men generously and without reproaching, and it will be given him.
days.refl: Couples who long for a child face many decisions: which doctors to see, which tests to take, how much to spend, when to rest and when to keep going. Advice comes from every side, and some of it pulls against what we believe. St. James tells us that God gives wisdom generously and without reproaching, without making us feel foolish for asking. Today we ask Him for clear minds, good doctors and the wisdom to choose well together.
days.more: The Church encourages medical care that seeks and heals the causes of infertility (CCC 2375; Dignitas Personae 13). She teaches that methods which take the conceiving of a child out of the marital embrace, such as IVF, are not morally acceptable (CCC 2376–2377). This is hard teaching, given out of love for marriage and for the child. Every child, however conceived, is a gift from God, and His mercy is open to every couple.
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, Giver of wisdom, guide N. in every choice before them. Lead them to doctors who are skilled, honest and kind, and give them courage to choose what is right even when it is hard. Through the prayers of St. Joachim and St. Anne, keep them united in each decision, free them from fear and pressure, and give them peace in every choice that is right in Your sight.
days.step: Write down the questions you want to ask a doctor or a priest, and pray over them together before you go.

days.title: Children We Have Lost
days.verse: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted, / and saves the crushed in spirit.
days.refl: For some couples, the waiting has included a pregnancy that ended too soon. A miscarriage or a stillbirth is the loss of a child, and the grief is real, even when others do not see it or quickly move on. The psalmist tells us that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted; He does not keep His distance from our grief. Today we bring to Him every child lost before we could hold them, and every hope that ended in sorrow, and we ask Him to comfort us.
days.more: The Church entrusts children who die without Baptism to the mercy of God, who desires all to be saved, and Jesus’ tenderness toward children gives us reason to hope for them (CCC 1261). It can help to give a name to a child you have lost and to entrust them to God by name. If this has not been your story, pray today for those who carry it.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You took the children in Your arms and blessed them. We entrust to Your mercy every little one N. have lost, each one known to You by name. Comfort them in their grief, heal what is still raw, and do not let them carry it alone. Through the prayers of Our Lady of Hope, who stood by the Cross of her Son, and of St. Anne, keep us all in the hope of the resurrection.
days.step: If you have lost a child, speak their name to God today, or choose one. If not, pray for a couple who carries this grief.

days.title: A Love That Bears Fruit
days.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me, and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
days.refl: Jesus tells us that whoever abides in Him bears much fruit. That promise is for every disciple, and it holds for every marriage, whether or not God sends children. A couple who stays close to Christ bears fruit in ways they may not yet see: in the love they share, the welcome of their home, the young people they guide and the people they serve. Today we ask to stay close to Him, and to trust that our love is never wasted.
days.more: The Catechism says that physical sterility “is not an absolute evil,” and invites couples to unite this cross with Christ’s (CCC 2379); a marriage without children can still be full of meaning (CCC 1654). Some couples are called to adoption or fostering, which the Church warmly encourages; others become godparents, mentors or a second home to many. None of this cancels the longing; it gives it room to bear fruit.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, true Vine, keep N. close to You. Make their love fruitful in every way You choose: in their care for each other, in the welcome of their home, and in the lives they touch. If You are calling them to welcome a child in another way, give them open and generous hearts. Through the prayers of St. Joachim and St. Anne, let nothing of their love be wasted.
days.step: Talk together about one way your love already reaches beyond the two of you, and thank God for it.

days.title: Into God’s Hands
days.verse: Have no anxiety about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which passes all understanding, will keep your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
days.refl: St. Paul does not tell us to stop asking. He tells us to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, and he promises a peace beyond understanding, not an answer on our timetable. On this ninth day we still ask for the gift of a child, and we place that request in the Father’s hands. We also thank Him for what He has given along the way: each other, the people who stood by us, and every moment when He was near.
days.more: Zechariah’s long silence ended in a hymn of praise, the Benedictus, which the Church still prays every morning (Luke 1:68–79). Mary, the daughter of Joachim and Anne, would one day give her own yes to God’s word (Luke 1:38). Whatever God’s answer, no prayer offered in love is wasted. We can end this novena and begin it again as often as we need.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, we thank You for these nine days and for every grace You have given N. along the way. We place their longing for a child in Your hands once more, trusting in Your love and Your wisdom. Through the prayers of Our Lady of Hope, St. Joachim, St. Anne and St. Zechariah, give them Your peace, keep their love strong, and let Your will be done in their lives.
days.step: Write down three graces you noticed during these nine days, and thank God for them together.
